sections.html:
Peabody is a city in Essex County on the North Shore, about 15 miles northeast of Boston and 2 miles from the center of Salem. Wikipedia lists 16.81 square miles of area and an elevation of 16 feet.

The city is wedge-shaped, with the center in the wider northeastern end. South Peabody lies south of the center, and the more suburban West Peabody, where the high school sits, lies to the west beyond the highways and the Proctor neighborhood. Neighbors are Middleton, Danvers, Salem, Lynn and Lynnfield.

The Ipswich River forms the northwestern border and the Waters River drains the northeast. Low-lying lots near those waterways deserve a flood question before you sell.

Peabody was settled in 1626 as part of Salem and later belonged to Danvers. It split off in 1855 as South Danvers, took the Peabody name on April 30, 1868 in honor of the philanthropist George Peabody, and became a city in 1916.

Leather defined the economy for generations, and the city is still called the Leather City and the Tanner City. Tanneries drew immigrant workers, and by 1915 one third of residents had been born abroad. Tanneries have since closed or moved. Earlier, the Central Street corridor was a hub of redware pottery in the eighteenth century, and Walnut Street, known as Ottoman Street, filled with boarding houses for workers from the Ottoman Empire.

The early twentieth century brought cars as well: Corwin Manufacturing, a Brass Era automaker, was based here.

On October 28, 1915 a fire at St. Johns School killed 21 young children, and Peabody became the first city in the country to require public buildings to have push-open exits. The city's population doubled between 1950 and 1970, from 22,645 to 48,080, so a large share of its homes date from that postwar growth.

sections.h2: What does the Peabody economy look like?
sections.html:
Peabody replaced its tanneries with retail, health care and technology employers. The Northshore Mall opened in September 1958 as an outdoor shopping center, and Centennial Park, an industrial park in the middle of the city, has drawn medical and technology companies.

Employers named on the city's Wikipedia entry include:

  • Lahey Hospital and Medical Center and Boston Children's Hospital
  • Analogic, JEOL, Carl Zeiss and UTC Aerospace Systems
  • Saucony, Christian Book Distributors and Meridian Interstate Bancorp
  • The Northshore Mall

West Peabody was mostly farm land until the 1950s and has since developed into a middle-to-upper class residential area, in the entry's words.

sections.h2: What do the numbers say about Peabody housing?
sections.html:
The 2020 census counted 54,481 residents in 22,315 households and 23,191 housing units, with 3.8% of units vacant. The table uses figures from that census as reported on Wikipedia.

Nearly a quarter of residents are 65 or older, and 31.2% of households are one person. Older owners and estates are a natural source of local sales.

sections.h2: What are Peabody's tax rates and how do you reach the assessors?
sections.html:
The City of Peabody's Assessors Office page lists FY26 property tax rates of $9.47 for residential and $18.85 for commercial property. The page also links to a cyclical inspection program FAQ, property value information, real estate exemptions and a Property Tax 101 guide.

The assessors can be reached at 978-538-5716. Two things are worth checking before a sale: whether an exemption on your bill ends with the transfer, and whether the cyclical inspection program has a visit scheduled for your address. Quarterly due dates and lien certificate steps come from the city collector, whose page we did not open for this guide, so ask that office directly.

sections.h2: How do highways and transit connect Peabody?
sections.html:
Highways include Interstate 95, Route 128, Route 129, U.S. Route 1 and Route 114. Several MBTA bus lines pass through town. The closest commuter rail stop is in Salem, on the Newburyport/Rockport Line to North Station, and the nearest airports are Beverly Municipal and Boston's Logan.

The Peabody Municipal Light Plant, owned by the city, provides electricity. National Grid supplies natural gas, and Comcast and RCN hold cable licenses. Transferring electric service to a new owner therefore runs through a city utility, which is a small difference from most Massachusetts towns.

Independence Greenway, a 5.25 mile rail trail, and Brooksby Farm, a 275-acre city-owned farm and conservation area, give the city green space that buyers often ask about.

sections.h2: What state steps apply when selling in Peabody?
sections.html:
A Peabody seller needs an alarm certificate from the fire department. The Department of Fire Services says to call for the inspection as soon as a closing date exists, and to expect a fee.

An attorney handles the closing and the recorded deed, since the Trial Court Law Libraries describe attorneys as part of Massachusetts sales by law and by practice. Deed excise is set by Chapter 64D, Section 1. Sellers of certain residential properties also cannot condition acceptance of an offer on a waiver of a home inspection under 760 CMR 74.

A direct purchase follows the same legal path, and you may still need to clear a mortgage payoff, estate paperwork or a lien before the deed records.

sections.h2: Who runs Peabody and which schools serve it?
sections.html:
Peabody has a mayor-council government, and Edward A. Bettencourt Jr. is listed as mayor on the city's Wikipedia entry. Peabody Public Schools run Brown, Burke, Carroll, Center, McCarthy, South, Welch and West elementary schools, Higgins Middle School and Veterans Memorial High School, whose teams are the Tanners.

Private options include Bishop Fenwick High School, Covenant Christian Academy and St. John the Baptist School. We list names only. The district confirms which school a given address feeds.

sections.h2: What neighborhoods and parks come up when sellers talk about Peabody?
sections.html:
Sellers and buyers tend to describe Peabody by section.

  • The center and Peabody Square in the northeast.
  • South Peabody, with Tillie's Farm, a city-owned farm.
  • West Peabody, home to the high school.
  • The Proctor neighborhood between the center and the west.

Other local landmarks include the Peabody Institute Library, established in 1852 after a bequest from George Peabody, the North Shore Children's Museum and Crystal Lake, a 21-acre conservation area. The Washington Street Historic District is a nineteenth-century residential area. If your house sits in a designated district, ask the city whether any local rules apply.

sections.h2: When does a cash sale make sense in Peabody?
sections.html:
A cash sale can fit when you want a firm closing date and do not want to prepare a house for the market. The legal steps stay the same: the fire department certificate, a payoff for any mortgage and a deed recorded at the registry.

  • Estates in which heirs live out of state.
  • Houses needing roof, heating or electrical work.
  • Owners facing a move on a short schedule.

Tell us what the house needs and who has to sign, and we can describe how an offer would line up with those documents.

faqs.q: What are Peabody's property tax rates?
faqs.a: The Assessors Office page lists FY26 rates of $9.47 residential and $18.85 commercial. Confirm the unit and your own bill with the assessors.

faqs.q: Who do I call about Peabody property assessments?
faqs.a: The Assessors Office lists 978-538-5716. The page also links to exemption information and a cyclical inspection FAQ.

faqs.q: Does Peabody run its own electric utility?
faqs.a: Yes. The municipally owned Peabody Municipal Light Plant provides electricity, while National Grid provides natural gas.

faqs.q: Is there commuter rail in Peabody?
faqs.a: No station is listed in the city. The nearest commuter rail service is in Salem on the Newburyport/Rockport Line.

faqs.q: Do I need a smoke and CO certificate to sell in Peabody?
faqs.a: Yes. Mass.gov says a sale needs a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing alarms meet requirements.
